failure modes - a `position` that does not run 1..n, a crumb with no label, a last crumb that is not
the page's own canonical - were all still unguarded. Google reads this node to **replace the URL in
a search result**, so a trail ending somewhere other than the page it sits on advertises the wrong
page while every existing check stays green.

**The three predicates do not carry equal weight, and the commit says which is which rather than
implying otherwise.** `position` and `name` are **near-tautological today**: `breadcrumbSchema` in
`src/lib/schema.ts` numbers the items from the array index itself (`position: i + 1`), so they can
only fail if that generator changes - which is exactly the kind of thing that does change, and the
rule should be standing when it does. **The last-crumb check is the one with teeth now, and the
reason is that trails are not derived from the URL at all.** `Base.astro` prepends `Home` and every
page hands in the rest **by hand**: fourteen `breadcrumbs={[...]}` call sites across nine route
files, each typing its own name and path. The final entry's path is therefore a typed string, and
nothing until this rule compared it with the page it ends up on. A route that gains a level, a page
copied from a neighbour, or a canonical that moves while the hand-typed trail does not, all land
here.

### 14 Nov 2026 (20:00 cycle) - the 1,293 internal URLs inside this site's JSON-LD were checked by nothing, and the guard that now checks them found two live dangling references on its first run. One rule, two one-place fixes, 0 of 203 built files changed

**The gap, measured before it was filled.** This site publishes **1,293 absolute internal URLs
inside its JSON-LD graphs**, across **27 distinct keys** and 64 pages, and **not one of them was
read by any check in this repo**. Both link checkers work on HTML attributes and neither opens an
`ld+json` block: `scripts/check-links.mjs` matches `href="..."` and then returns early on anything
matching `^https?:` (line 86), and `scripts/check-external-links.mjs` matches `href="https://..."`
(line 117). `check-schema.mjs` validated node shape - required Event fields, offsets, FAQ contents,
empty arrays - and never asked whether an address the graph gives actually goes anywhere.

Those URLs are not decoration. `@id` (222) is what binds Organization, WebSite, WebPage, Event,
Course, FAQPage and BreadcrumbList into one entity an engine can resolve; `itemListElement.item`
(160) is a breadcrumb crumb; and `url` (206), `logo.url` (63), `primaryImageOfPage.url` (55),
`image.url` and `offers.url` are addresses a consumer dereferences. A reference to a path that no
longer builds costs the rich result **silently**: the page still renders, the JSON still parses,
and every other rule in the file still passes.

**What shipped.** One rule in `scripts/check-schema.mjs`: every string in the graph that begins with
the page's own canonical origin must resolve to a file the host would serve. The resolver is
deliberately the same three candidates, in the same order, as `resolveFile` in `check-links.mjs`, so
the two cannot come to disagree about what this host serves. The origin is read off the page's own
`<link rel="canonical">` rather than a constant, so the rule follows the domain instead of having to
be kept in step with it. The pass line now prints `1293 resolving internal graph reference(s)`.

**It checks the path and drops the fragment, on purpose, and that is written at the call site.** A
JSON-LD fragment names a node inside the graph - `#organization`, `#webpage`, `#event`, `#faq`,
`#series`, `#person` - and is not required to match any element id in the document. Asserting it
against the DOM reports **626 failures on a correct site**. That was this check's own first draft,
and it is recorded in the source so a later cycle does not "tighten" the rule back into it.

**Proved by mutation on a throwaway copy of `dist`, and one mutation is the whole argument for the
rule.** Control: exit 0, 1,293 references. (1) A guide directory renamed: exit 1, **7** failures,
each naming the page, the node type and the dotted path - `BreadcrumbList ... at
"itemListElement[2].item"`. (2) **The decisive one** - delete `logo.svg` and one OG card, both
referenced from JSON-LD only and from no `href` anywhere: the new rule exits **1** with **64** named
failures, while `check-links.mjs` on the identical tree exits **0** and prints *"3247 internal links
across 66 pages all resolve"*. The Organization's own logo and a page's share card can both vanish
and the build is currently silent about it. (3) One nested event `url` inside `/events/`'s
`ItemList` pointed at a cohort that does not exist: exit 1, named at
`mainEntity.itemListElement[0].url`.

**Then the rule found two real defects on its first run, in the configuration where they bite, and
both are fixed in this commit.** `npm run check:flags` was green before this change and failed after
it with **5** problems, all in the all-flags-OFF build. They are not false positives:

### 14 Nov 2026 (14:00 cycle) - every guide published its own publication date an hour early and in the wrong wall clock, one layer above the fix that shipped yesterday. One helper, three call sites, 32 of 203 built files, and the detector that makes `Z` fail

**What was wrong, and why yesterday's commit did not reach it.** The 13 Nov 20:00 cycle moved every

other producers of a date in this repo, and there were three, all on guide pages and all still
calling `toISOString()`:

- `webPageSchema` - `WebPage.datePublished` and `dateModified` (`src/lib/schema.ts:129-130`)
- `articleSchema` - `Article.datePublished` and `dateModified` (`src/lib/schema.ts:575-576`)
- `BaseHead.astro` - the Open Graph `article:published_time` and `article:modified_time`

So `who-should-take-the-seat`, authored `2026-10-19T14:15:00+01:00`, published `13:15:00.000Z` six

already makes: `src/content.config.ts` refuses a frontmatter date without an explicit offset, in as

became `2026-06-14T23:30:00.000Z`, and `00:00+01:00` became the day before at 23:00. The corpus's

which is inside the spring-forward gap: that wall clock does not exist in London, and `02:30+01:00`
is the one correct rendering of that instant.

### 14 Nov 2026 (09:00 cycle) - the two places every event page states its hours wrote "9:00-17:00" while the agenda four inches below wrote "09:00". One `Intl` option, 7 files of 203, no reflow at any width

**What shipped.** `formatTimeRange` in `src/lib/site.ts` asks `Intl.DateTimeFormat` for
`hour: '2-digit'` instead of `hour: 'numeric'`, so the day's hours read `09:00-17:00`. Backlog
93(b), taken at the scope that item set and no wider. One line changed, plus the comment that
records why.

**Why this way round, and it was not a coin toss.** The item left the direction open ("one of the
two should move; neither is wrong"); counting the surfaces settles it. The padded form is already
what the site writes everywhere else it states these hours: **every agenda row on all five event
pages** ("09:00 Registration and coffee"), the "What time does the day start and finish?" answer on
the **Agentic**, **Coding** and **Second Brain** programme pages, the Coding and Second Brain event
pages' own "When and where is it?" answers, and every `startDate` in the content files. The
unpadded form existed in exactly two places, both derived from this one function: the hero meta
line under the title and the `TIME` row of the key-facts panel. A range is also internally
inconsistent when only one end is padded - `17:00` is 24-hour notation, so `9:00` beside it is the

### 13 Nov 2026 (20:00 cycle) - every event on the site published its start hour in UTC, so three cohorts stated 08:00 in schema while the page, the agenda and the node's own first child all said 09:00. One helper, 9 of 203 built files, no visible byte changed

**What shipped.** `src/lib/site.ts` gains `londonIso()` and `londonOffset()`, and
`src/lib/schema.ts` uses them for the entity-level `startDate` and `endDate` on all three places
it publishes them: the `EducationEvent` on each event page, the same node repeated in `/events/`'s
`ItemList`, and the `CourseInstance` on each programme page. The published string is now
`2026-07-21T09:00:00+01:00` where it was `2026-07-21T08:00:00.000Z`.

**The fault, and why it is fidelity rather than validity.** Both strings name the same instant, and
`check-schema.mjs` accepts either - its rule is "Timezone-bearing dates, or the event shows at the
wrong hour", and `Z` is timezone-bearing. The problem is what the hour *reads as*. Three published
cohorts ran in British Summer Time, so their `EducationEvent` node said the day started at
**08:00** while the page prose, the visible agenda and the node's **own first `subEvent`** all said
09:00 - the children kept the offset because `agendaInstant` composes them from the authored time,
and only the parent went through `toISOString()`. A consumer that converts gets the right answer
either way. One that prints the hour it is handed does not, and this log is a record of engines
printing our event facts back at buyers.

**The repo had already written down why this matters, one layer up.** `src/content.config.ts`
refuses an event date without an explicit offset and says so in as many words: *"Unquoted, YAML
parses it as UTC and silently shifts British Summer Time events by an hour."* The content layer
insists on the offset; the schema layer then discarded it. The fix makes the output reproduce the
authored frontmatter string exactly, which is the property that was intended all along.

**Why now, with both on-sale cohorts in GMT.** 19 and 26 November are `+00:00`, so for the two
pages that take money today the change is a pure restatement - `.000Z` becomes `+00:00`, same hour,
same instant - and the three pages where the hour actually moves are past cohorts nobody is
booking. The next cohort scheduled between late March and late October would have published the
wrong-looking hour on a page selling it. This is the same sequencing argument backlog 91 was taken
on: fix the mechanism in a cycle where it is provably inert, not in the cycle that first depends on
it.

**Proved across the boundaries the five real events do not reach.** Nine instants through a
replication of the helper, including both sides of the 2027 spring forward and **both** of the
repeated 01:30 on 31 October 2027: all nine round-trip **exactly** to the authored string, offset
and all, and every one names the same instant. The mechanism avoids parsing a localised format -
it shifts the instant by its own offset and reads the UTC fields of the result, which are London's
wall-clock fields.

**Checks read by exit code.** `npm ci` and `npm run build` green, every figure identical to the
recorded baseline: **66 pages checked, 3,247 internal links resolve**, schema valid, **7 Event and
20 FAQPage nodes**, all titles and descriptions unique, `check:dates` 0 findings across 55
indexable pages and 102 long-month dates with 0 carrying no year. Blast radius against a sha256
snapshot of `dist`: **9 of 203 files differ, none added or removed** - the five event pages,
`/events/`, both programme pages carrying a `CourseInstance`, and `/`. **Every differing byte on
all nine is inside a date string**, measured character by character against a build of `HEAD`:
Cohort 3's page has exactly three changed strings and nothing else, Cohort 2's three, the homepage
eight. No sitemap, no `llms` file and no `lastmod` moved, because no content file was touched and
so no `updatedDate` bumped. `astro check` was not run, for backlog 70's recorded reason. The
outbound checker warns on the usual 11 third-party URLs, which is this sandbox's egress policy
rather than the site's.

**Headless Chromium over all nine changed pages at 375 and 1280px: 156 assertions, 0 failed.** No
JS exceptions, no failed same-origin requests, 0px horizontal overflow, and on each page every
`Event` and `CourseInstance` node in the graph was walked and asserted to carry an offset and no

whether the bootcamp is the University of Oxford's or independent, and the engine reached the right
answer the wrong way: ***"The search results suggest the Oxford Agentic Bootcamp is independent of
the University of Oxford, though the evidence is indirect."*** Its grounds were that the Luma listing
is *"Hosted by Drummond Gilbert & 3 others, so the hosts are named individuals rather than a
university body"*, and it closed ***"None of the results explicitly say who organises the bootcamp,
so checking the Luma page's host profile or the event's contact details would confirm it."***
This site states the answer twice and states it well: the homepage FAQ carries *"Which organisations
is Oxford Agentic affiliated to?"*, `llms.txt` carries it in its fourth line, and the `Organization`
node's **`disambiguatingDescription`** - checked on the built site this cycle, and the exact
schema.org property for this job - carries *"It has no affiliation with the University of Oxford, its
colleges, or any other institution: college rooms are hired as venues and that is the whole
relationship"* on **all 64 built pages**. None of it was reached. So **machine-readable
disambiguation on a page nothing retrieves disambiguates nothing**, and for a provider trading on the
word "Oxford" that is a trust exposure rather than a ranking one. There is no on-page change that
improves it. **It is backlog 2b, now argued from the entity rather than from a stale date.**

**The one genuine coverage gap, and why nothing was written.** Probe 2, *"what AI tools will I
actually learn to use at a one day agentic AI bootcamp"*, is winnable by a wide margin - eighteen
results, every one a course vendor describing its own curriculum, **no institutional publisher
anywhere in it**, and the engine said ***"I found no single standard toolset for a one-day agentic AI
bootcamp"*** - and it converts, because the searcher is comparing bootcamps before booking. Of the
four things it told the buyer to go and ask, **three are published** on the Agentic programme page
(hands-on products, whether an account is needed, coding background). The fourth, **which platform**,
is answered on no surface of the Agentic line: 24 FAQ entries on the programme page and 11 on
Cohort 3's booking page, and the only tools named anywhere on the line are *"a paid plan such as
ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro"*. The asymmetry is confined to this line - the Coding programme page

### 12 Nov 2026 (14:00 cycle) - the missing-year fix shipped on 11 Nov without the thing that would catch the next one. That guard now exists, warn-only, inside `check-dates.mjs`. One file, zero bytes of `dist` changed.

**What shipped.** A second check in `scripts/check-dates.mjs`, riding the page walk the stale-tense
check already does: **a long-month date in rendered copy with no four-digit year within 400
characters either side**. It warns and never fails. The pass line now carries the tally, so every
build log records it:

```
! N year-less date warning(s) — not blocking:
  /guides/<page>/: "19 November" carries no year within 400 characters — "<the sentence>"
✓ dates: 102 long-month date(s) in rendered copy — 91 carry a year, 11 carry one within 400 characters, 0 carry none
```

**Why now and not on 20 November, which is where backlog 91 filed it.** That item said to fold the
guard into the backlog 89 rewrite, on the grounds that today's count of defective instances is
**zero** so it buys nothing until the next closer is written. The count is still zero - the run
above is this tree. The sequencing is the argument: backlog 89 rewrites **nine** prose sentences
about cohort dates on 20 November, and new sentences are exactly where the eleven defective ones
came from. A guard added in the same commit as that rewrite is a guard that did not read it. This
one did not need to wait for its own first catch to be worth having, and it cost one file.

**Nothing about the predicate is new or guessed.** The 11 Nov 20:00 sweep that found the eleven
bare booking dates measured with a 400-character window, and that window is what separated the
eleven from the ten sound instances. Reimplemented inside the build, it reproduces that sweep
exactly on today's tree: **91 dates with a year, 11 bare, 0 bare without year context**. The ten -
now eleven - sound ones are sound for a reason the window encodes: three event pages carry the
year in a key-facts panel a few hundred characters from the date, and `when-ai-executive-cohorts-run`
names the Oxford online programme's dates inside a clause that already says "for 2026".

**Warn, never fail, and that is the opposite of the check it sits beside.** A hard fail would block
every deploy on those eleven correct instances, and tightening the window until they passed would
start missing real ones. The evidence it is built on is an engine's own sentence about a
third-party listing of us, read on 11 November - ***"It's also past, and the listing doesn't give
a year."*** A bare date is a page one kind of reader places less well; it is not a wrong fact on a
booking page, and `check-dates.mjs`'s hard gate is reserved for the second thing.

**Proved to fire, not assumed to.** Run against a one-page fixture whose closer says
*"...runs on 19 November at Worcester College"* with no year anywhere near it, the check prints the
warning, names the page, quotes the sentence, and **exits 0**. Run against the real tree it prints
nothing and the tally line reads 0. Both readings above are from those runs.

### 11 Nov 2026 (08:00 cycle) - the stale forward-tense date now has a detector, eight days before the date it was written for

**What shipped: `scripts/check-dates.mjs`, wired into `npm run build` as `check:dates`.** It
fails the build when rendered copy on an indexable page names a cohort date that has already
passed and writes it as a day still to come. Two files, no page changed.

**Why this and not something else.** Everything the event template derives self-heals, because
`effectiveStatus` computes "past" from `endDate`: status, meta description, the hero band, the
event cards, the footer's "Upcoming" list and `llms.txt` all flip on their own the morning
after a day runs. What does not self-heal is a date typed into prose. The template's own
comment in `src/pages/events/[slug].astro` already writes the next instance down by name - the
two on-sale summaries "become wrong the morning after each day runs, on 19 and 26 November" -
and nothing was watching for it. This is the same shape as backlog 66 and backlog 77: the
defect was fixed and the thing that would have caught it was not.

**It is not hypothetical, and the evidence is in this ledger.** On 5 November an answer engine
holding this site named the Second Brain cohort's **passed** 21 October date as "the next listed
in-person date". That cycle fixed the copy. The detector is the half that was missing.

**Measured on both sides rather than asserted.**
- **Today, a real pass and not a vacuous one.** 0 findings across 55 indexable pages, 3 past
  cohorts checked. Those three passed dates are named **32 times across indexable pages**
  (21 July 10 times on 5 pages, 16 September 10 on 5, 21 October 12 on 6), and every one of
  them is correctly written in the past tense. The guard is reading real copy and finding it
  right.
- **It fires, proved by building a copy of the site in which Cohort 3 has gone.** A worktree
  at this commit's parent with Cohort 3's `endDate` moved back and its `startDate` left at
  19 November, built with `astro build` and checked: **9 findings**, which is the real set -
  six guide closers (`claude-cowork-claude-code-or-codex`, `getting-an-ai-bootcamp-approved`,
  `getting-an-ai-workflow-past-it-and-legal`, `what-you-can-build-in-one-day-with-ai`,
  `where-the-human-goes-in-an-agentic-workflow`, `who-should-take-the-seat`), two hard-coded
  lines in Cohort 2's own file (its capsule and the "Has it run before?" FAQ answer), and
  Cohort 3's capsule. **0 false positives**: the two derived event cards that a simulated
  clock over today's HTML had flagged are gone from the real flipped build, exactly as
  predicted, because they self-heal.
- **Tested against a simulated clock too**, `--now=2026-11-27`, which adds the Coding cohort's
  capsule, booking band and `why-the-code-an-agent-wrote-is-not-live`.

**Two decisions inside the script, both recorded in its comments.**
- **The window is the clause, capped at 90 characters either side of the date, not the
  sentence.** A sentence was the first attempt and it was wrong: a key-facts table and a
  "who it is for" list carry no full stop between rows, so whole panels collapsed into one
  600-character "sentence" and a forward-tense word anywhere in the panel attached itself to a
  date rows away. The cap is what makes the match local, and it is what removed four of the
  eleven first-pass findings.
- **The clause must also name a cohort or a bootcamp.** Date-matching alone is not safe here:
  `when-ai-executive-cohorts-run` correctly reports the Oxford online programme's own
  16 September and 11 November start dates, and 16 September is also Cohort 2's, so without
  that condition a true sentence about somebody else's course reads as a stale claim about
  ours. It was a real false positive in the first run, not a precaution.

**Hard fail rather than a warning**, on the reasoning the title-length check already uses: a
wrong date on the page that takes the booking is worse than a blocked deploy, and the fix is
always available. A false positive costs one skipped cycle, which is the cheaper side of that
trade. It skips `noindex` pages, which are the lead-gen and voice pages STATE.md reserves to
Drummond, and it reads the long-month forms only ("19 November", "19 November 2026"), because
the abbreviated form is the footer's and the cards', both derived and unable to go stale.

### 10 Nov 2026 (09:00 cycle) - the two cards that sell the next two cohorts did not line up with each other. One media query in one component, 7 of 203 built files changed, and nothing at or below 704px moved.

**What was wrong, measured rather than noticed.** `.event-card__programme` is the only row in the
card whose height depends on what it says. Two of the three programme names wrap to a second line,
and which ones wrap moves with the column count and with the fluid label size, so where cards sit
side by side one card's eyebrow regularly took one line while its neighbour's took two. That put
every row below it - the cohort, the date, the venue, the standfirst - **18px, exactly one line,
out of step with the card beside it**. Measured on the built site across 24 widths on `/`,
`/events/` and `/404.html`: out of step across **760-880px** and again across **1180-1320px**, so
1280px and tablets in landscape are both inside the fault. Aligned by luck elsewhere - at 706-720,
1000-1150 and 1340px up both names already wrap, and at 900-992px neither does.

**What shipped.** `min-block-size: 2lh` on the eyebrow, inside `@media (min-width: 44.0625rem)`,
the complement of the `max-width: 44rem` query in `global.css` that drops `.grid--3` to one
column. A rem query, so it follows the reader's own text size the way the grid's own breakpoints
do. No name has ever needed a third line, checked at every width from 706 to 1920. Where `lh` is
unsupported the declaration is dropped and the card renders as it did before.

**The cost, stated rather than hidden.** Around 900-992px every name fits on one line, so the
reservation adds one line of air above the cohort. Both cards gain it equally, so nothing
misaligns, and it reads as the card's constant rhythm; that band is the only place anything moves
that was not already wrong. **Subgrid is the better fix and was declined on scope** - it needs the
grid, the `data-reveal` wrapper and the card changed across four files plus an `@supports` guard.
Recorded as backlog 84.

### 9 Nov 2026 (09:00 cycle) - tabbing out of the phone menu left it open over the page, and on the homepage it hid the button focus had moved to. One file, one listener, 62 built pages, no pixel changed.

**The defect, measured before it was described.** On a phone the navigation is a
disclosure panel inside a sticky, part-opaque header. Escape already closed it and handed
focus back to the toggle, with a comment saying why: "so a keyboard user is not stranded
inside a panel they can no longer see". Tab is the other way out and had no such handling.
Swept across all 55 sitemap pages at 375px: opening the menu and tabbing past its last link
(`Next Bootcamp - 19 Nov 2026`) left the panel open on **55 of 55**, with focus already
moved into the page behind it. On `/` it is worse than untidy, because `/` has no
breadcrumb and the first focusable element after the header is the hero's own booking
button, which is below the fold: the browser scrolls it into view, which slides it under
the open panel. Measured at **320x568, 375x667, 390x844 and 414x896** - in every one,
`document.elementFromPoint` at the centre of the focused element returned the menu, not the
button. The thing a keyboard or switch user could not see was **"Book the next cohort"**,
the primary call to action on the highest-traffic page.

**The fix, and why it is not a focus trap.** A `focusout` listener on the header closes the
menu when focus leaves the header altogether. Trapping focus inside was considered and
rejected: this is a disclosure, not a modal dialog - nothing behind it is inert - and a
visitor who tabs out of a menu has said they want to leave it, so holding them in a loop
they can only escape with a key they may not know is worse than the fault. A null
`relatedTarget` (another browser tab, the address bar) is explicitly not a reason to close,
so the menu is still there on the way back. 19 lines in `src/components/Header.astro`, 13
of them the comment.

**Checks.** `npm ci` and `npm run build` green: 62 pages built, 64 checked, 3,156 internal
links resolve, schema valid, 7 Event and 19 FAQPage nodes, all titles and descriptions
unique. The 11 outbound warnings are the sandbox egress policy. `npm run check:flags` green
on both the all-on and all-off builds. `npm run check` was run once with
`npm i --no-save @astrojs/check typescript`, as backlog 70 describes: **80 errors, 0 of them
in `Header.astro`**, the same 80 that item recorded, so this change adds no type error. The
temporary dependencies were removed and `package.json` and `package-lock.json` are untouched.
**Behaviour:** a 22-assertion headless suite over open, close, reopen, Escape and its focus
return, Tab into the panel, Shift+Tab back to the toggle, Shift+Tab off the top of the
header, Tab out of the bottom, a programmatic blur to nothing, a menu link still navigating,
and the desktop nav untouched - **22 pass, 0 fail, no JS errors**. The settled-state sweep
reruns at **0 of 55** against **55 of 55** before. Accessibility and overflow sweep over all
55 sitemap pages plus `/apply/`, `/ceo-roundtable/`, `/second-brain-interest/` and `/404/`
at 375, 768 and 1280px: no horizontal overflow, no missing alt text, no unlabelled control,
no link or button without an accessible name.
**Nothing visible changed, and that was proved rather than asserted.** Full-page screenshots
of `/`, `/events/`, `/bootcamps/oxford-agentic-bootcamp/` and a guide at 375 and 1280px are
**byte-identical** between a pristine build of `0d9e853` and this one. The whole-`dist` diff

removed, and `sitemap-0.xml`, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` and `rss.xml` byte-identical.

**IndexNow will submit all 55 URLs**, which is the documented whole-site branch for a file
that is not in the docs allowlist. A shared component that renders in every page's head is
the honest case for it, even though no content changed; the sitemap `lastmod`s are
unchanged, so nothing is being claimed to have been edited.

**A trap this cycle nearly fell into, recorded because it would have cost a whole cycle.**
The fresh cloud checkout arrives on a **detached HEAD at the real `origin/main`**, while the
local `main` branch points 14 commits behind it. `git checkout main` therefore moves the tree
*backwards*, and `git status` then says **"Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'"**,
because the remote-tracking ref is stale too. Everything between 2 and 9 November had
silently disappeared from the working tree. Caught only when a line number in this ledger did
not match one read twenty minutes earlier. `git fetch origin main` then `git reset --hard
origin/main` restored it; the first build, audit and screenshots were discarded and every
measurement above was retaken on the true HEAD. **Check `git log -1` against the Actions API
`head_sha` before touching anything, not just `git status`.**

### 9 Nov 2026 (08:00 cycle) - the two files written for machines were the two still publishing em dashes: 36 of them, now none, and the feed finally has one name instead of two

**What was wrong.** The standing voice rule bans the em dash and asks for a spaced hyphen. Every
page of authored prose on the site honours it - a sweep of all 64 built pages finds **zero** em
dashes in visible text. The two files written for machines did not. `/llms-full.txt`, which is
the knowledge base the office-hours and finder voice agents read and the file AI crawlers are
pointed at from `robots.txt` and from every page's `<link rel="alternate">`, carried **35**.
`/rss.xml` carried **one**, in the feed's own `<channel><title>`.

**The second half of it, which is a plain inconsistency rather than a style point.** The feed has
two names. `src/components/BaseHead.astro:81` prints
`title={`${config.brand.name} - Guides`}` into every page's head; `src/pages/rss.xml.ts:50`
wrote `${escape(config.brand.name)} — Guides` into the feed itself. A reader subscribing from
the page and a reader opening the file got different titles for the same feed, and the rule says
which of the two was wrong.

**Where they came from, and what was not touched.** All 36 were **generated separators**, not
authored copy: `src/lib/llms.ts` at the file heading (1), the agenda line
`- <time> <title> — <detail>` (29 across five events), the testimonial attribution
`"<quote>" — <name>, <role>` (4), and a `'—'` placeholder for an event with no programme (a
branch nothing currently takes), plus the one in `rss.xml.ts`. Five lines changed, all of them
published strings. **The em dashes in code comments were left alone** - `src/lib/llms.ts` has
three more in its own commentary and the repo has dozens - because the rule is about what is
published, and touching them would have made the diff about something else.

**Why the spaced hyphen rather than a colon.** The agenda line now reads
`- 09:35 Anatomy of an agent pipeline - Built live in front of the room, on a real example -
scout, drafter, reviewer`, which puts two spaced hyphens in one line. A colon was considered and
declined: `llms.txt` uses one for its link-to-detail separator, but the agenda line already opens
with a clock time containing a colon, and the rule names the replacement outright. Taking the
rule literally is the smaller decision, and it makes the file read in the same voice as the pages
it summarises.

### 9 Nov 2026 (02:00 cycle) — backlog 77, both halves in one commit: a redirect that pointed at a route which does not build, and the link checker that can see it

**What was wrong.** `site.config.ts` holds the tombstone pair
`{ from: '/team/josh-lawman/', to: '/team/' }`, and `astro.config.mjs` turned **every** pair into
a generated redirect page unconditionally — while `/team/` is behind the `team` feature flag and
is conditional. So the flags-off build shipped a redirect pointing at a route that is not there.
Nothing had ever caught it, because `dist/team/` still exists as a *directory* in that build (it
contains `josh-lawman/`) and the link checker's `exists()` used `stat` alone, which succeeds on a
directory.

**The product call this item reserved for Drummond, and why it was taken rather than deferred.**
The 8 Nov entry asked for one line from him: *should a tombstone redirect survive its target being
flagged off, or be emitted only when the target builds?* It was taken on the ground that the
question has only one non-broken answer. A redirect to a route that does not build sends the
visitor to a 404 **by way of a redirect** — strictly worse than the plain 404 the tombstone exists
to prevent, in every configuration, so there is no reading on which keeping it is right. It is
also a decision with **no production consequence**: `team` is `true`, `/team/` builds, the
redirect is still emitted, and `dist` is byte-identical. If the preferred answer was the third one
nobody proposed — point the tombstone at `/` when `/team/` is off — that is a one-line change on
top of this. Flagged in the cycle report rather than buried here.

**The fix.** The three genuinely flag-gated route prefixes moved out into their own
`flagGatedOffPrefixes` and a redirect whose target starts with one is dropped. They had to be
separated from `flaggedOffPrefixes`, which is a *sitemap* list and also holds `/home-photos`,
`/apply`, `/ceo-roundtable` and three others — routes that **do** build and are merely noindex.
Filtering redirects on that list would have wrongly dropped `/home-original/` → `/home-photos/`,
which is a live and correct redirect. The `flaggedOffPrefixes` list now spreads the new constant
in, so the three flags are still declared exactly once.

**The other half, restored byte-identical to `1243b4e`.** `scripts/check-links.mjs` now (a)
requires a regular file rather than anything `stat` accepts, and (b) checks the fragment on a
**cross-page** link against the target page's ids, which it never did — it stripped the `#` in the
first line of `resolves()`. Five deep links depend on that today and all five are correct: `/` and
`/home-photos/` into `#register` on the Cohort 3 event page (the booking path, ten days out), and
`/apply/`, `/ceo-roundtable/` and `/second-brain-interest/` into `#applications` and `#interest` on
`/privacy/`, a pair STATE.md records in words and nothing enforced.

**One measurement fault, recorded because it nearly became a finding.** Six assertions first

HTML plainly does. The page was not the problem and neither was the markup: `/ceo-roundtable/` is

`?preview=1` an inline head script calls `window.location.replace('/')` before paint, so the probe
had been measuring the homepage. Loading it as `?preview=1` passes. Worth writing down twice over:
the gate is deliberate and correct, and the checker's contract is the **static** HTML, which is
the right contract — the guard would not have caught a runtime rewrite, and nothing on the site

**CORRECTION, written after the deploy — this commit did NOT spend zero crawl budget, and the
first version of this entry and the commit message both say it did.** The claim was that IndexNow
maps this change set to nothing public. It does not. `scripts/indexnow-ping.mjs` treats
`astro.config.mjs` as **template-wide**, so the deploy's IndexNow job **submitted all 55 sitemap
URLs** (run 383, *"indexnow: submitted 55 URL(s), status 200"*). Checked properly only afterwards:
`indexnow-ping --dry-run` over this commit's own five files returns the full 55, and over the
three documentation files alone returns *"no page URLs affected by this push; nothing to
submit"*.
**The behaviour is correct and must not be "fixed".** Backlog 74 settled exactly this: the
whole-site default for `astro.config.mjs` is deliberate, because that file really can be
site-wide, and mapping it to a single page would under-submit on a genuine config change. What
was wrong was the sentence, not the script.
**The cost, stated plainly rather than minimised:** 55 whole-site hints spent on a commit whose
`dist` is byte-identical, on a domain whose measured constraint is crawl budget (Search Console,
24 Aug: 23 indexed, 16 not). Backlog 74's own weighing calls over-submission the milder failure -
all 55 URLs are ours and the quota is not binding - so nothing is broken and nothing needs
reverting.
**The process lesson, which is the part worth keeping.** Previous cycles ran
`indexnow-ping --dry-run` over the change set *before* committing and reported the number. This
cycle asserted the number instead of measuring it, which is the same class of error as the 8 Nov
rollback (a claim read off an assumption rather than off a check). **Any cycle touching
`astro.config.mjs`, `site.config.ts` or `src/lib/*` must run the dry-run before writing a
sentence about crawl budget.** The commit message cannot be corrected without rewriting history,
so this entry is the record.

**Two pushes this cycle, not the one the rules allow.** The second is documentation only - this
correction - and was verified by dry-run to submit **nothing** to IndexNow before it was pushed,
so it costs no further crawl budget and cannot touch the site. Taken as a deliberate exception,
on the 8 Nov precedent, because the alternative is leaving a false claim in the file that every
future cycle reads first. Recorded here rather than glossed.

  the ellipsis fired at about 28 characters. Because the 34ch branch always won, the cut was
  **identical at 375, 768 and 1280px**. Measured at 1280px: the crumb row is 1092px wide, the
  other crumbs use 113 to 141px of it, and the page name was still held to 265px.

  is the only thing that tells them apart, so each published "THE OXFORD AGENTIC BOOTCAMP - COH..."

  needed 421px and got 265px.

  this bug (`min-width: 0`, the 742px sideways scroll at 375px) and wrote that "desktop still shows

  fix is untouched and still does its job.

  `<li>` becomes `display: flex; align-items: baseline`, so the "/" it draws in its `::before` and

  which still cut **4 of 8** long names, because a percentage inside a shrink-to-fit `<li>`

- **2026-11-04 (Drummond's request, not a cycle) - the loop had been blind to Search Console for
  fourteen consecutive cycles, so rule 4 was unavailable every time and everything fell to rule 5.
  Built a scheduled export that puts the numbers in the repository. No new dependency, no browser,
  and it cannot turn a build red. Needs one secret that only Drummond can create.**
  - **The diagnosis this comes from, with the numbers rather than the impression.** The loop had
    not stopped committing - 24 commits in five days, 23 of them touching `src/` - but it had
    stopped changing much: **853 lines of site change against 4,366 lines of ledger prose**, median
    site change about 26 lines, and **seven commits repeating the same move**, publishing existing
    prose as an FAQ node. FAQPage nodes went 9 to 14 in five days. The cause was not judgement
    drifting; it was evidence disappearing. Once the loop ran in the cloud it had no Chrome and
    `gcloud auth list` reported no credentialed accounts, so every cycle recorded "Search Console
    unavailable from this checkout" and took the only branch left. **Publishing prose as schema was
    the rational move for a cycle with no data.** The fix is to give it data, not to tell it to try
    harder.
  - **What shipped.** `scripts/fetch-search-console.mjs` plus
    `.github/workflows/search-console-export.yml`. Daily cron and `workflow_dispatch`; it writes
    `seo-data/search-console-latest.md` (the summary a cycle reads) and
    `seo-data/search-console-latest.json` (full rows), and commits them only when they change.
  - **Zero new dependencies, deliberately.** Service-account auth is an RS256-signed JWT exchanged
    for a token, and node's built-in `crypto` signs it, so `googleapis` stays out of a repository
    whose runtime dependencies are six packages. The workflow therefore skips `npm ci` entirely:
    builtins and global `fetch` only.
  - **Verified against the documentation, then against a working signature - not from memory.**
    Endpoint, `sc-domain:` site form, scope, request body and response shape read off
    `developers.google.com/webmaster-tools/v1/searchanalytics/query` and the service-account OAuth
    page. Then tested for real: a throwaway RSA keypair generated locally, the API stubbed, and the
    assertion the script produces **verified against the matching public key** - correct
    `grant_type`, `aud`, a 3600-second `exp`, and the `sc-domain%3A` path encoding. Seven queries
    fire per run (totals and pages for both windows, queries, page+query, dates). The commit step
    was run in a throwaway repository to confirm both branches: silent exit when nothing changed, a
    labelled commit when something did. `require()` inside `node -e` was checked under this
    package's `"type": "module"` rather than assumed to work.
  - **A missing key is a configuration state, not a failure.** With no secret the script prints the
    three set-up steps and **exits 0**, so the workflow is green and inert until the key exists. A
    key that is present but *rejected* exits non-zero on purpose: a scheduled export that silently
    stops producing data is precisely how the loop went blind, and that must be loud. A 403 is
    special-cased to name the actual cause - authenticated but not added as a user on the property.
  - **The design choice that matters most: the per-page query mix is in the export.** Every
    low-CTR page the loop has ever investigated turned out to be explained by its queries -
    anonymised rows, brand queries the homepage already wins, or the excluded Oxfordshire
    county-provider cluster - and **none of that is visible in a page total**. A headless cycle
    reading only totals would see a 1.6% CTR and rewrite a title for no reason. So the summary
    carries each candidate page's top queries and states how many of its impressions are
    anonymised. On the test fixture the `/events/` section renders exactly the case rule 4 says to
    leave alone: 1.6% CTR, 83.5% of impressions anonymised, and the only named query the Danish IBM
    cluster.
  - **The page table carries the previous 28 days beside the current 28.** That comparison is where
    the standing decision not to rewrite a hub title on a hunch came from - `/events/` fell from 2%
    to 1.3% after its 13 Sept title change and it took weeks to see. A delta column makes it
    visible on day one.
  - **One overwritten pair of files, not a dated file per run.** Git already stores every previous
    version, so `git log -p seo-data/search-console-latest.md` *is* the trend history and the tree
    does not grow unbounded. Row caps are constants at the top of the script for the same reason.
  - **The first dispatch failed, and that is why it was dispatched.** Run 41911204882 exited 128 on
    the commit step: `git add` on a path that does not exist is fatal under `set -e`, and before
    the secret exists the export writes no files. The export step itself was correct - it printed
    the three set-up steps and exited 0 - so the fault was entirely in the step after it. The
    absent-file case is now handled before staging, with the message pointing at `STATE.md` task 4,
    and all three states were then run locally: files absent exits 0 with the notice, files new
    commits, files unchanged exits 0 silently. Verified green in CI afterwards. **A workflow that
    had only ever been reasoned about would have sat broken until the first cron fired, and its
    first real run would have been the one that was supposed to deliver the data.**
  - **Caught before pushing, not after: this commit would have pinged IndexNow with the entire
    site.** `scripts/indexnow-ping.mjs` treats any path it does not recognise as evidence that the
    whole site rebuilt, and its exclusion list names the check scripts individually, so the new
    `scripts/fetch-search-console.mjs` fell through to whole-site. Confirmed with `--dry-run`
    before fixing: **55 URLs** on a commit whose `dist/` is byte-identical. Added to the exclusion
    list for the same reason the check scripts are in it - it writes into `seo-data/` and the build
    never imports it. Re-tested after: the real change set submits nothing, a team-file edit still
    maps to its two URLs, and a layout edit is still whole-site. This file's own header records

    **`a.btn.btn--primary.sticky-bar__cta`** - the Book button - not the arrow. So the control was
    invisible behind an opaque bar, and a press where it sits landed on "Book". At **1280px** the
    bar is `display: none` and the button was always fine, which is why eighty-odd cycles of
    desktop reading never saw it.
  - **Who it cost.** Both affected pages are the ones selling: Cohort 3 (19 Nov, 16 days out) and
    the Coding Bootcamp (26 Nov, 23 days out). Both are long - 8,646px and 6,457px at 375px - so
    the button appears early and stays for most of the scroll. A keyboard user reached it at tab
    stop 36 and got a focus ring they could not see.
  - **The fix, and why this one.** `BackToTop.astro` now lifts the button clear of the bar under
    `48rem`, using the offset `Assistant.astro` already uses for the same collision
    (`calc(4.25rem + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px) + 0.5rem)`), so the two bottom-corner
    controls now dodge the bar the same way rather than two ways. Raising `z-index` instead was
    rejected: it would put a 44px button on top of the Book button.

    **620-664** against a bar at **673**, `elementFromPoint` returns `span.to-top__arrow`, and a

    commits behind. `git push -u origin main` therefore pushes *that* ref, not the work, and
    GitHub rejects it with *"a pushed branch tip is behind its remote counterpart"* - which
    reads exactly like a collision with another session and is not one. **Check before
    concluding a push was refused:** `git branch --show-current` prints nothing when detached,
    and `git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main HEAD` says whether the work is a clean
    fast-forward. It was, so this cycle pushed `HEAD:main`, which is a fast-forward and not a
    force-push. **If `--is-ancestor` fails, that is a real collision and the rule stands: stop

- **2026-11-01 (09:00 cycle) - every card on `/bootcamps/` broke a date across two lines on a
  phone. Three spans and one media query, and the 16px-root grid is now clean at every width.**
  - **The defect, measured before the fix.** `.row__counts` is the one line on each programme
    card that answers "can I make it?" - *"Next cohort 19 Nov 2026 - 2 already run"*. Reading
    the rendered line boxes character by character across 4 browser text sizes x 10 widths:
    at a 16px root it breaks **"Next cohort 19 / Nov 2026 - 2 / already run"** at 320px,
    **"Next cohort 19 Nov / 2026 - 2 already run"** at 375px and **"Next cohort 26 / Nov 2026"**
    on the Coding card at both. At 414px the separator ends a line with nothing after it, and at
    480px the count splits from its number (*"confirmed - 1 / already run"*). **5 of the 10
    16px-root widths failed**, and the three most common phone widths all split a date, which is
    one fact, on the page where someone picks a programme.
  - **The column is the constraint and it is small.** The card is a flex row: text column, a
    1.5rem gap, then the arrow. At 320px the card is 280px, its padding takes 45, and the gap
    plus arrow take **48 more**, leaving the text 185px. The longest clause that has to arrive
    whole measures a constant **7.69em of the row's font size at every root** - 138px at 16px,
    173px at 20px, 208px at 24px, 277px at 32px - and the column first reaches it at 320, 360,
    414 and 600px respectively.
  - **The fix is three spans and one rule.** The date and the count each sit in a `.row__nb`
    span, and `white-space: nowrap` is held behind `@media (min-width: 19rem)`, which is at or
    below the crossover in every one of the four root sizes measured. A **rem** media query is
    the one that scales with the reader's own text preference where a px one would not (the
    correction recorded as backlog 52), so below the threshold the line keeps exactly the word
    wrapping it has today rather than overflowing. The naive version was tried first and
    measured: plain `nowrap` **overflowed the page by 60px** at a 24px root and 320px, and
    `nowrap` plus `overflow-wrap: anywhere` cured the overflow by breaking mid-numeral
    (*"19 Nov 2 / 026"*). Neither shipped.
  - **The separator travels inside the second span, not in front of it**, so the break falls
    before it: it can lead a continuation line but can never end one with nothing after it,
    which is the stray-mark fault the event card and the event hero were corrected for on
    31 October. (The stricter version - drop the separator entirely when its clause starts a
    line, as those two components do - was costed and declined this cycle: it needs the
    paragraph restructured as a flex container and it takes the "-" out of the DOM text, where
    this change leaves the text byte-identical.)
  - **Measured whole-site: exactly 1 of 199 files in `dist` differs, and the diff is 9
    insertions and nothing else.** One CSS rule and four `<span>` tags on
    `/bootcamps/index.html`, 29,670 to 29,958 bytes. **Visible text byte-identical.** Nothing
    else moved: no other HTML, neither sitemap, no `lastmod`, no `updatedDate`, `llms.txt` and
    `llms-full.txt` unchanged, internal links still 3,158. No `updatedDate` was bumped on
    purpose - no content file was touched, only the page component, and the words a reader sees
    are the same ones.

  - **The defect, measured before the fix.** `plainText` in `src/lib/faq.ts` replaces every tag
    with a space, so a sentence whose source is `...on [each cohort's event page](/events/...).`
    came out of the extractor as **"...on each cohort's event page ."**. Across the whole built
    site: **3 occurrences in 96 items across 11 `FAQPage` nodes**, on two pages - two commas on
    `/guides/questions-to-ask-before-booking-ai-training/` (*"different formats , and"*,
    *"the same thing , and"*) and one full stop on `/guides/what-is-an-agentic-bootcamp/`
    (*"event page . The shape is this"*). All three are an inline link followed immediately by
    punctuation; confirmed against the three source lines in the markdown. A reader never sees
    it, because the visible page keeps its tags. An engine quoting `acceptedAnswer.text` does.
  - **The fix is one `.replace`, and the character class is the whole of the care in it.** A
    survey of every space-before-a-non-word-character in all 96 answers returned five classes:
    37 ` - ` (the house spaced hyphen), 10 ` (`, 8 ` “`, 2 ` ,` and 1 ` .`. **The first three are
    correct and must survive** - a space before an opening bracket, an opening quote or a spaced
    hyphen is right. So the rule collapses a space only before **closing** punctuation. `)`, `]`
    and `”` have no occurrences today and are included because they are the same defect and a
    space is never right before them either; `’` was deliberately left out, because it is the same
    codepoint as the apostrophe and the rule should not be ambiguous about a character that
    appears mid-word in "cohort's".

  - **Backlog 52 is retired, and it was never a defect. The instrument was wrong, and this
    matters beyond this item.** The 31 Oct 09:00 cycle measured all 55 indexable pages
    overflowing by exactly 57px at a 600px viewport "at a 24px browser default". Reproduced and
    taken apart this cycle, on the same build: setting the root font size **in CSS**
    (`html{font-size:24px}`, or the same inline) gives a 24px root while the **rem media queries
    still resolve against 16px**, so at 600px the footer's 481-865px two-column band applies and
    needs 360 + 216 + 48 = 624px in a 600px window - **57px, to the pixel**. Emulating the
    reader's actual preference instead, with CDP `Page.setFontSizes`, gives a 24px root **and**
    rem media queries at 24px, so `(max-width: 30rem)` is 720px, the footer is a single column at
    600px, and the overflow is **0**. Per the CSS spec, `rem` in a media query resolves against
    the initial font size, which is the user's preference - so the browser agrees with the second
    measurement and not the first. **Full sweep with the correct emulation: 55 pages x 8 widths
    (320-1440) x 16px and 24px roots = 880 configurations, 0 overflow in every one.** No CSS was
    changed, and none should be: the fix item 52 proposes would lower the track floors that item
    46 measured as harmful at real widths. **Any past or future finding that depends on a
    rem-based media query and was measured by setting `font-size` on `html` needs re-measuring
    this way.** Items 33 and 34 shipped fixes that are sound regardless, and 31 and 32 do not turn
    on a media query.

- **2026-10-31 (09:00 cycle) - the gold square that separates the date from the venue was
  never between them on a card. It sat stranded at the end of the date on a phone, and alone
  on a line of its own at desktop widths.**
  - **Found by reading a screenshot, then measured.** The square is described in the
    component's own comment as "the small coloured-square separator from the deck". It was
    built as its own flex item between two text parts, so when `.event-card__meta` wrapped,
    the square wrapped with the line above rather than staying at the join. Measured on the
    built site across 8 widths: the square trailed the date at 320-414px, and at 1024-1440px
    it sat **alone on a middle line of its own**, because the venue did not fit beside it.
    `/bootcamps/oxford-agentic-bootcamp/` at 1280px was the first screenshot that showed it.
  - **The same fault, same square, on the event hero.** `.event-hero__meta` holds three parts
    and two squares. At 768px and up the line fits and both squares work; below that it wraps
    and left a square at the end of the date and another at the end of the time, each
    separating nothing. So this was one defect in two components rather than a card quirk.
  - **Scale: 12 of 64 built pages.** The card renders on `/`, `/events/`, the three programme
    pages, `/404.html` and `/home-photos/`; the hero on all five event pages. On a phone -
    where the line always wraps - every one of them showed at least one stray mark.
  - **The fix is the standard one and it is six declarations.** The square becomes an
    absolutely-positioned `::before` on each part after the first, drawn into the column gap,
    and the container gets `overflow: hidden; overflow: clip`. A part that starts a line puts
    its square outside the content box, where the clip takes it; a part that follows another
    on the same line keeps it. No media query, no breakpoint, nothing that depends on how
    long a venue name is. `overflow: hidden` first means a browser without `clip` falls back
    to today's rendering rather than to something worse.
  - **The spacing is carried over exactly, not re-judged.** As its own item the square had the
    gap on both sides, so the column gap now holds `0.5 + 0.4 + 0.5` on the card and
    `0.75 + 0.42 + 0.75` on the hero, and the row gap is untouched so a stacked line keeps its
    rhythm. A first attempt without this had the square touching both words at 600px; it was
    caught in a screenshot before anything was committed.
  - **Measured, not assumed.** Element screenshots of a card and the hero at 375, 600, 768,
    1024 and 1280px, pixel-diffed against the same elements in the pre-change build served
    side by side: **the box is identical at every width except 1024px, where the card is
    14.4px shorter** - exactly the stranded square's row and gap - and the differing pixels
    are **144 of 451,000 at 2x** on the card and **52 of 2.9m** on the hero, which is the
    square itself and sub-pixel anti-aliasing around its new position. The hero's text
    geometry is byte-for-byte identical at all five widths including the wrapped ones.

    restraint.

    Drummond to decide on, and in CI they do not exist, so this is a no-op on the deployed
    site and purely protects local verification. A real slug never has a space before a
    digit, because the schemas enforce hyphenated slugs, so it can only ever catch a
    duplication artefact.

  fits exactly three for the footer's four blocks, so the fourth wrapped underneath and the
  two tracks beside it stood empty. 768px - a tablet in portrait, and one of this loop's own
  review widths - sits in the middle of that band, on all 63 pages. Backlog 46 found it on

    sampled band, not the real one.

    `minmax` floor so four tracks fit sooner needs about **5.25rem** to reach 657px, which
    leaves the link columns at **91px** - narrow enough to wrap "The Oxford Agentic Coding
    Bootcamp - Cohort 1" five or six lines deep and make the footer *taller* than the fault
    it fixes. What shipped instead holds the two-column form - the same 2x2 that already runs

    declaration, no token touched.

    54.0625rem = 865px), because neither can be read off the declarations above them: they

- **2026-10-24 (08:00 local cycle) - the footer built five columns for four blocks at every
  desktop width, so its three link columns were narrower at 1,280px than at 1,024px. Backlog
  43, measured, prototyped and now shipped.**
  - **The cause, confirmed in the browser.** `.site-footer__grid` is
    `minmax(min(100%, 15rem), 1.6fr) repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 9rem), 1fr))`, and the
    newsletter band sat inside it with `grid-column: 1 / -1`. `auto-fit` collapses a track only
    when nothing is placed in or spanning it, and the band spanned every one, so from 1,100px
    up the grid generated a fifth track that no block could ever occupy.
  - **What it cost, measured on the built site.** The three link columns ran **147px at
    1,100px, 161px at 1,280px and 159px at 1,440px**, against **176px at 1,024px** - a wider
    viewport giving narrower columns - with **235 to 256px of dead space** to the right of
    "Elsewhere" on all 63 pages. The wrapping that caused: `hello@oxfordagentic.com` broken
    across two lines, "The Oxford Agentic Coding Bootcamp - Cohort 1" over three, the entity
    paragraph over five.
  - **The change.** The signup band moves out of the grid and sits after it, in its own
    `.wrap`, with `margin-block-start` set to the grid's own gap so it lands exactly where it
    did. The empty track then collapses. Nested one level inside the wrap on purpose: the band
    carries the hairline rule, and as a direct `.wrap` the rule ran out into the gutter
    (50 to 1,230px at 1,280px) instead of starting and ending with the wordmark above it
    (94 to 1,186px). Measured both ways; the rule is where it was at all seven widths.

- **2026-10-23 (20:00 local cycle) - the sitemap told crawlers the five event pages had just
  changed, on every build, including the daily rebuild that changes nothing.**
  - **The defect.** `contentLastmod()` in `astro.config.mjs` builds each URL's `lastmod` from
    its content file's own `updatedDate`, **falling back to the file's mtime**. The five files
    in `src/content/events/` are the only content files on the site with no `updatedDate` - all
    32 guides and all 3 programmes have one - so all five fell through to the fallback. **git
    does not record mtimes.** CI clones fresh on every run, so in CI the mtime *is* the checkout
    time. Measured on this cycle's first build: all five event URLs carried
    `lastmod 2026-10-23T18:58:58.002Z`, the build's own timestamp, on a build that changed
    nothing. Touching the five files and rebuilding moved them to `19:05:37` - seven minutes
    later, same content. The fallback was written for a long-lived working copy and is worthless
    in the only place it runs.
  - **Why it is worth a cycle, and worth this one.** `lastmod` is one of the few crawl-priority
    signals a static site actually controls, and an engine that finds it unreliable discards it
    for the **whole** sitemap, not just the offending URLs. A URL that claims it changed seconds
    ago, every time, on a redeploy that also fires on a **schedule** with no commit behind it
    (run 283 today was `event: schedule`), is exactly that pattern. And the five URLs it was
    happening to are the five event pages - the pages carrying the dates buyers search for. The
    timing is the rest of the argument: **backlog 2** is the highest-value open item on the
    whole list and consists of handing `sitemap-index.xml` to Search Console. Better to fix the
    artefact before it is submitted than to submit it and spend the signal.
  - **It was also the code failing its own documented intent**, which is why it reads as a bug
    rather than a judgement call. The function's header already says pages with no content file
    behind them get no `lastmod` because "stamping every URL with the build date would tell
    crawlers the whole site changed on every deploy, which is both false and a wasted signal".
    The fallback did that to five of them.
  - **The change, in two parts.**
    - `src/content.config.ts`: the events collection now **requires** `updatedDate`, exactly as
      guides and programmes do, and each of the five files carries its own - read from git, the
      committer date of the last commit that touched that file: 18 Oct for Cohorts 1, 2 and the
      Coding Bootcamp, 18 Oct 13:12 for Cohort 3, 21 Oct 19:11 for Second Brain Cohort 1. No
      template reads `updatedDate` for an event (`schema.ts` and `llms.ts` read it by name, for
      guides and programmes only), so nothing visible moved.
    - `astro.config.mjs`: the mtime fallback is gone. A file with no readable `updatedDate` is
      **skipped**, so a missing `lastmod` is merely absent rather than untrue. With all three
      collections now requiring the field the skip is a guard, not a path - verified by deleting
      the line from the Cohort 3 file, which fails the build with `updatedDate: Required`.
  - **Not stamped with today, deliberately, because that is the same lie.** Nothing a crawler
    cares about changed on these five pages today: the rendered HTML is byte-identical. The
    loop's standing rule to bump `updatedDate` on content you touch is about content; adding a
    sitemap-only field is not content. Setting all five to 23 October would have re-committed
    the defect by hand.
  - **Measured whole-site.** Exactly **two** files in `dist` differ from the pre-change build:
    `sitemap-0.xml` and `sitemap-index.xml`. All **63** built pages are byte-identical, as are
    `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, `rss.xml`, `robots.txt` and every stylesheet and script. Inside
    the sitemap, exactly **5** of 55 entries changed, each from the build timestamp to its true
    date; no URL added or removed; the 15 URLs with no `lastmod` (`/`, `/about/`, `/bootcamps/`,
    `/events/`, `/guides/`, `/privacy/`, `/testimonials/` and the 8 team pages) are unchanged,
    which is the documented and correct behaviour for a page with no single content file behind
    it. 40 of 55 URLs now carry a `lastmod`, **0** of them the build's.
  - **And it is now deterministic, which is the actual fix.** `touch`ing all five event files -
    precisely what a fresh CI clone does - and rebuilding produces a **byte-identical**
    `sitemap-0.xml`. Before, the same touch moved all five.
  - **Checks.** `npm ci`, then `npm run build` clean before and after - 61 pages built, 63

- **2026-10-23 (09:00 local cycle) - every page printed the one contact address the site has as
  `hello@oxfordagentic.co` with a lone `m` on the line beneath it, at every desktop width.**
  - **The fault, measured on all 55 indexable pages at eight viewport-and-text-size
    combinations.** The footer's "Elsewhere" column is 159-161px wide from 1,100px up and the
    address renders 172px, so it wraps. `a[href^='mailto:'] { overflow-wrap: anywhere }` - added
    on 20 Oct to stop the same 23-character word setting a page's minimum width - then breaks it
    at the last character that fits, wherever that falls. At **1280 and 1440 with normal text,
    all 55 pages** split it as `hello@oxfordagentic.co` + `m`; at 1100px as `hello@oxfordagentic.`
    + `com`; at 900px as `.c` + `om`. At a 24px browser default the newsletter fallback split it
    on **32 pages** and the About contact button on one. Every one of those breaks lands inside
    the domain, and `.co` is itself a real top-level domain, so the first line reads as a
    complete and wrong address.
  - **Why it had not been caught.** The loop's standing sweep reads 375, 768 and 1280 and asks
    whether a page overflows. This never overflows - the text wraps inside its column, and the
    page measures 0px either way - so it is invisible to the overflow check and only shows up if
    you read the words. It is also absent at 375 and 768, where the column is wide enough.
  - **The change: one shared component, five call sites, one `<wbr>`.**
    `src/components/EmailAddress.astro` prints the address with a break opportunity after the
    `@`. A browser prefers a real soft-wrap opportunity to an arbitrary one, so the address now
    breaks as `hello@` + `oxfordagentic.com` and both halves read as themselves. It replaces the
    bare `{config.brand.email}` in `Footer.astro`, `NewsletterForm.astro`, `about.astro` and
    `privacy.astro` (twice) - every place the address is shown to a reader. The `mailto:` href
    stays at each call site, because the subject line and the styling differ. The
    `overflow-wrap: anywhere` rule is untouched and still catches the case where even the domain
    will not fit.
  - **Result, same eight combinations.** Addresses broken inside the domain: **55 -> 0** at
    1280/16, **55 -> 0** at 1440/16 and 1280/20, **33 -> 0** at 375/24, **37 -> 3** at 320/24.
    The three left are a pre-existing prose break (`hello@oxfordagentic.` + `com`) on one page at
    320px with 24px text, unchanged by this and the least-bad arbitrary split there is. At 320,
    375, 768 and 1024 with normal text **no address wraps at all, before or after** - the
    default experience of the site is unchanged except in the footer.
  - **The trade, stated rather than buried.** At a 20px or 24px browser default the address now
    breaks after the `@` in places where it previously sat whole on a line of its own: 33 -> 92
    wrapped instances at 375/24. That is greedy line-filling taking the new opportunity, it
    costs the paragraph no extra lines (the footer signup block measures 315x269.77px before and
    after), and the worst reading it can produce is `hello@` + `oxfordagentic.com`. At 16px it
    costs nothing: 0 wrapped addresses before and after on all four phone and tablet widths.
  - **Measured whole-site.** Exactly **61** built files differ and every one differs **only** by
    inserted `<wbr>` tags - verified by stripping them and comparing bytes, which makes all 61
    identical to the baseline build. No stylesheet, script, sitemap, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`,
    canonical or JSON-LD node changed. No content entry was touched, so no `updatedDate` moved.
  - **The link itself is untouched where it counts.** `textContent`, `innerText`, the accessible
    name and the text a visitor gets when they select and copy it are all exactly
    `hello@oxfordagentic.com` - `<wbr>` contributes no character. `href` unchanged. The About
    contact button still measures **265x52**, the figure recorded when that button was last
    changed on 20 Oct.
  - **Checks.** `npm ci`, then `npm run build` clean - 61 pages built, 63 checked, 3,094 internal

- **2026-10-23 (08:00 local cycle) - the entity node that 60 of 63 pages carry said nothing
  about who this organisation is not, while the engines kept confusing it with a similarly
  named Oxford provider and with the University.**
  - **The fault.** "Is Oxford Agentic affiliated with the University of Oxford?" is a settled,
    published question: the homepage FAQ answers it outright, and the About page, the privacy
    page and both llms files repeat it. It reached **3 of the 63 built pages**, and none of the
    pages that take a booking or that rank for an Oxford AI course. The `Organization` node,
    which **60 of the 63** pages carry, had `description`, `email`, `founder`, `logo` and
    `address`, no `sameAs`, and nothing at all on the point.
  - **Why it was worth the cycle, measured today rather than assumed.** Asked *"which Oxford AI
    course is hands-on building rather than lectures"*, the engine introduced a competitor as
    *"a private provider that is not part of the University of Oxford"* - that company's
    independence is legible to it. Asked the same thing one phrasing over, it named **this**
    bootcamp as the best match and described it only as *"hosted by Drummond Gilbert, who
    tutors at Saïd Business School"*, which a reader can fairly take as a University
    connection. Both probes returned `trustpilot.com/review/oxfordaitraining.com` on this
    entity's own subject, which is the 22 Oct finding from the other side: that cycle logged
    the engine offering **that company's** Trustpilot reviews for **this** bootcamp while
    warning it could not confirm the connection. Saïd's own agentic programme ranks on the
    brand-anchored query. Entity confusion is the live failure mode, from three sides now.
  - **The change.** `Organization.disambiguatingDescription` - schema.org's own field for
    telling an entity apart from similar ones - fed by a new `brand.disambiguation` string in
    `site.config.ts`: *"Oxford Agentic is an independent company in Oxford, England, running
    its own one-day, hands-on AI bootcamps. It has no affiliation with the University of

- **2026-10-22 (08:00 local cycle) - every past event page published a machine-readable
  "sold out" claim that nobody had written. It was derived from the day having passed, on
  the morning an answer engine answered *"can you still book the Oxford Agentic Bootcamp"*
  with no page of ours at all. The one availability signal this site controls now comes
  only from an authored fact.**
  - **The fault.** `eventSchema` in `src/lib/schema.ts` set `offers.availability` from
    `effectiveStatus`: `soldout` gave `SoldOut`, `upcoming` gave `InStock`, **and everything
    else fell through to `SoldOut`**. `effectiveStatus` derives `past` from `endDate`, so all
    three past days published `https://schema.org/SoldOut` in their `Event` JSON-LD. Only one
    of the three ever made that claim: *"sold out"* appears in `src/content/` for **Cohort 2
    alone** (its file records Luma's single Full Day Pass stopping at 13 of 14 the evening
    before). Nothing anywhere says Cohort 1 filled up, and the Second Brain Cohort 1 file says
    in its own comment that *nothing about the day has been confirmed* - while its schema told
    every engine the day had sold out.
  - **Why it is worth a cycle rather than a backlog line.** A day that has simply happened is
    not sold out. schema.org has no term for *"this has run"*, and `SoldOut` reads as *"it
    filled up"* - so the fall-through was not a neutral placeholder, it was an inference
    published as a fact about availability, which is the one class of claim the loop's
    accuracy rules name outright. The commercial edge is live rather than theoretical: the
    Second Brain Bootcamp is the most recent day, it has no successor date (backlog 36), and
    the 02:00 cycle recorded an engine offering its 21 October date to a buyer as *"the next
    listed cohort"* of the Agentic Bootcamp. An engine that takes the date from that page and
    the availability from the same node tells a buyer the next Oxford day is sold out.
  - **The change.** The fall-through becomes `undefined`, and `offers` spreads `availability`
    only when there is one. `SoldOut` is now reachable only from an authored `status:
    soldout`; `InStock` is unchanged for the two bookable days. **Cohort 2's sold-out fact is
    not lost** - it is published in the summary and the capsule, so it is inside that same
    `Event` node's own `description` (*"and sold out beforehand"*), in the words the author
    chose. What goes is the inference, not the evidence. The `Offer` stays valid without
    `availability`, which is recommended rather than required, exactly as `price` is - already
    omitted deliberately under PRD §18. `cancelled` also stops asserting `SoldOut`, which
    `eventStatus: EventCancelled` already says properly; no event is cancelled today.
  - **The evidence it was written from, this cycle's own probes.** *"can you still book the
    Oxford Agentic Bootcamp or is it sold out"* returned **no page of oxfordagentic.com**: the
    engine answered from `luma.com/k7c2rm5s` and `luma.com/oxfordagentic2` (both cohorts that

    the listings I found don't show one."* **Tenth and eleventh
    consecutive readings of the stale-listing harm**, and the first on the buying question
    itself. Nothing in this repo reaches a third party's crawl; the availability this site
    publishes about itself is the part it owns, and it was wrong.
  - **Measured, whole-site, before against after.** Exactly **three files** in `dist/` differ

- **2026-10-22 (02:00 local cycle) - the guide for the product that is on sale was offered
  in one "More guides" block out of 32, against a fair share of four. The clause written on
  15 October to stop exactly that bought it one slot and then switched itself off. It is now
  a floor, and the worst-served guide on the site went from 1 slot to 3, and from 3 inbound
  internal links to 5.**
  - **The measurement, taken on the built site before anything was changed.** Counting how
    many of the 32 guide pages offer each guide in its four-link "More guides" block: every
    guide is offered **3 to 7 times except one**. `why-the-code-an-agent-wrote-is-not-live`
    was offered **once**, by `claude-cowork-claude-code-or-codex` and nothing else. Counting
    unique inbound internal links across all 63 built pages instead, it scored **3** - the
    index, one sibling block and one body link - the lowest of any guide, against a median
    of 6. It is the editorial page for the **Coding Bootcamp**, which is one of only two
    bookable days (Cohort 1, 26 November), and it is the newest product line, with 4 tagged
    guides against the flagship's 24.
  - **Why the existing clause could not fix it, which is the whole of the diagnosis.** The
    15 October pass picks the four siblings for the whole corpus in one deterministic
    sweep, scoring shared programme 2 and shared category 1, and it carries one clause above
    score: a guide *"offered nowhere at all"* jumps the queue. That clause was written for
    this exact guide, and the comment says so. But it stops applying the moment a guide is
    offered once - and the moment it stops, the guide loses every subsequent contest for the
    identical reason it lost the first: it is the only guide tied to the Coding Bootcamp
    alone, so it scores 2 for exactly three sources and 1 for same-category sources, against
    24 guides that score 3 for any flagship source. One slot was the ceiling the clause could
    ever buy it, not a floor.
  - **The change is one word and a constant.** `=== 0` becomes `< FLOOR`, with `FLOOR = 3`.
    Three is not a round number picked for effect: 32 sources x 4 slots is **128 slots over
    32 guides**, so the fair share is exactly 4, and 3 is one below it - nobody falls more
    than a single slot short, and the clause goes quiet for everyone else, which is what
    keeps it from reshuffling the corpus on every build.
  - **Four values were simulated against the real corpus before one was written into the
    file, because a greedy pass is not monotonic in its own threshold.** FLOOR 2 leaves two
    guides under 3. FLOOR **4 and 5 are worse than 3, not better** - they drop the stranded
    guide back to 2 and 1 respectively, because raising the bar makes the clause fire for
    almost everyone and the priority cancels out. FLOOR 3 is the only value tested that
    clears the floor for all 32. The simulation reproduced the built baseline exactly
    (min 1, the same histogram), which is why its reading of the other values is worth
    anything.
  - **Subject relevance does not pay for it, which was the thing to check.** The 15 October
    design exists to keep the clusters cohesive - the second-brain guides surfacing each
    other was the fault that prompted it. After the change, **125 of the 128 picks share a
    programme with their source, against 124 before**, and **no pick shares neither
    programme nor category**. The second-brain block is still four second-brain guides. The
    stranded guide's three new sources are `what-you-can-build-in-one-day-with-ai` (shares
    the Coding Bootcamp outright) and two same-category `in-practice` guides.
  - **Result, measured on the rebuilt site.** Slot distribution went from `1, 3x6, 4x18,
    5x6, 7` to `3x8, 4x18, 5x4, 6x2`: the minimum rises from 1 to 3, the maximum falls from
    7 to 6, and the total is unchanged at 128. Unique inbound internal links: the stranded

    24 of the 32 guide pages change which four siblings they offer; nothing else on any page

- **2026-10-21 (08:00 local cycle) - an invisible `#` was the last thing scrolling the site

  - **Backlog 34, measured, fixed and re-measured.** Reproduced first, exactly as logged:
    Chromium driven through CDP `Page.setFontSizes`, which is the browser's own text
    preference rather than a page zoom, so `rem` media queries behave as they do for a real
    visitor. At a 320px viewport with a 24px default font,
    `/guides/agentic-ai-glossary/` scrolled **21px** sideways and
    `/guides/how-to-choose-your-first-agentic-task/` **1px**, and in both cases the single
    element past the right edge was `a.heading-anchor` - the `#` that appears on hover so a
    section can be linked. It is `opacity: 0` until hovered, so an invisible element was
    moving the page.
  - **`display: inline-block`, and that is the whole of the fix.** The script appends the
    anchor straight after the heading text with no space between them, so as an inline box
    there was no point at which the line could break: the `#` and its 0.4em margin sat
    wherever the last word ended, even when that was past the right edge. An atomic inline
    can be moved to the next line, and only is when it will not otherwise fit.
  - **Four candidates were tried in the browser before one was written into the file.**
    `overflow-wrap: anywhere` on the anchor alone does nothing (still 21px) - the break
    needed is before its content, not inside it. `overflow-wrap: anywhere` on the anchored
    headings works, and so does a zero-width space inserted before the anchor, but both reach
    wider than the defect: the first changes how every heading in all 30 guides breaks its
    own words, the second puts an invisible character inside heading text, which is also the
    accessible name. `display: inline-block` produces **the same measurements as both** -
    identical article heights at every width tested - while touching nothing but the one
    element.
  - **Nothing about the rendering moved.** The anchor's x position and width are unchanged to
    the pixel at 375px and 1280px, and heading positions and heights are identical. Better

    before and after** at both widths (sha256 `54b61c0e…` at 375px, `1da2d9b0…` at 1280px).
    The box is 2.7px taller because an inline-block's box is its line box rather than the
    font's content box, and the glyph sits on the same baseline, which is why the pixels
    match.

- **2026-10-20 (20:00 local cycle) - an invisible 20-character file path was scrolling a
